items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang expected to be ousted
items.content_html:
After a second extramarital affair was uncovered, Nvidia's board is reportedly preparing to oust CEO Jensen Huang. Details of when and who might replace him aren't available.

Even as Apple faces increased scrutiny around its approach to AI, there are real problems brewing in the outer AI industry. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang admitted to an affair with someone accused of being a Chinese spy.

According to a report from the Wall Street Journal, a second extramarital affair coming to light Wednesday has forced the board to make a move. Huang could be ousted, though who might take over and the plan after are in question.

The AI industry was already seeing some deflation after investors lost trust that it would remain profitable. Google's results showing reduced ad revenue based on a shift to AI summaries didn't help.

Nvidia is a supplier of high-bandwidth memory and GPUs used in AI, so a downturn for AI hit the company too. However, it wasn't until the first affair came to light that the market reacted dramatically.

Over $800 billion was shaved off of the market cap of Nvidia in a day. The uncertainty around Nvidia's leadership has held the price down as the rest of the market adjusted to respond.

Apple remains above $5 trillion as its valuation isn't propped up on increasingly ambitious AI promises. It remains around $1 trillion higher than every other AI company it was said to be falling behind as soon as this week.

Nvidia will be fine in spite of this scandal. It remains to be seen if Huang's ousting is the final push that properly pops the AI bubble.

items.title: Apple employee charged with murder following fatal accident near Apple Park
items.content_html:
After an accident near the Apple Park Visitor Center, which resulted in the death of a toddler, an Apple employee was arrested and subsequently charged with murder.

On Friday, Apple employee Eric Chen Su reportedly drove at around 100 miles per hour as he crashed into a vehicle stopped in front of him. While Su sustained light injuries, the occupants of the vehicle he struck, a two-year-old and her babysitter, were rushed to a nearby hospital.

Although her babysitter survived, two-year-old Riley Howard unfortunately passed away from injuries sustained in the wreck. The incident occurred at 12:01 PM PT near the intersection of North Tantau Avenue and Pruneridge Avenue, near the Apple Park Visitor Center.

As The San Francisco Chronicle reports, Eric Chen Su was initially arrested and charged with suspicion of gross vehicular manslaughter. The charges against Su have since been upgraded to murder and assault with a deadly weapon.

According to KTVU, investigators found that Su's actions demonstrated disregard for the safety of people around him. "A reasonable person would know this time of day was busier than normal," investigators reportedly noted.

In a statement to MacRumors, Apple responded to the matter. "Our hearts are broken by the tragic accident that happened outside of Apple Park Visitor Center," explained an Apple spokesperson. "Our thoughts are with all of those grieving, and we are grateful for the care and support of the first responders."

While it remains unclear if Su has been placed on leave or if he was fired from Apple, the case against him will move ahead. 38-year-old Eric Chen Su is set to attend a plea hearing in Palo Alto on November 30.

items.title: You can now talk to Gemini right from Apple CarPlay
items.content_html:
Drivers can now ask Gemini to catch them up on unread emails or tell them when their next appointment starts.

On Wednesday, Google announced the rollout of Gemini to Apple CarPlay. And with Gemini Live, drivers can have back-and-forth conversations with Gemini while driving.

Drivers can tap the Gemini icon on the CarPlay display or side rail to start or resume a conversation. During a chat, they can interrupt Gemini, change the subject, or pause the conversation.

Conversations started in the car sync with the Gemini app on iPhone, allowing drivers to revisit them after parking.

Through Gmail and Google Calendar, Gemini can summarize unread messages and long email threads or check when an appointment starts. Gemini Live can also suggest places to eat or explain the history of a local landmark.

The rollout is worldwide and covers every language Gemini Live supports. Setup requires the latest Gemini app, microphone access, and at least one Gemini Live session on the iPhone.

This marks the second recent Gemini expansion onto CarPlay. In October, Google announced Gemini for Google Maps on CarPlay, allowing drivers and passengers ask Gemini questions using natural language.

items.title: Apple Support Communities were sound and fury, but sometimes so useful
items.content_html:
Maybe you used them to sound off, maybe you relied on fellow users to solve problems, and maybe, just maybe, Apple would answer questions on its support community forum. But no more.

Apple is shutting down its Apple Support Communities forum and for all that they could be frustrating, they will be missed. At least for now, they will remain online as a searchable repository of great answers to problems, terrible answers to them, and the odd argument.

But you'll never again be able to get into a proper discussion about an issue you thought was only bothering you. You'll never again be able to chat there about good or bad experiences with Apple.

You don't have to have used the forums to get the idea of what they were supposed to be for. You probably do have to have used them to recognize what is perhaps the most common recurring refrain in them.

That would be when someone would post about a problem and say that Apple has not acknowledged the issue. The phrases would differ and so would the problems, but you got used to complaints that there was this thing and Apple wasn't talking about it.

One reason for that could well be that, according to AppleInsider sources, Apple hasn't even been reading those forums for at least the last five years.

Maybe that made their eventual closure inevitable, or maybe John Ternus just doesn't want to have to keep adding storage space for it. But whatever the reason for their closure now and Apple's loss of interest long ago, it's all a far cry from when the company started these forums.

How it began

Strictly speaking, these forums began in 1998 under the name Apple Tech Exchange. But you can make a strong case that this really all began even longer ago.

Apple first launched forums when it opened AppleLink back in July 1985, although initially it was a resource for dealers and support staff.

According to "Apple Confidential 2.0" by Owen Linzmayer, a study at the time showed that Apple saved a minimum of $100 million per year ($314 million in today's money). That was through needing fewer staff, and greatly cutting the needs for travel, phones, and even paper.

So Apple became pretty keen on forums, although if you think it was making an easy saving, think again. Apple was paying in excess of $30 million ($94 million today) to GE for running it.

Still, anything that ends up with you saving a net total of $70 million has to be good. So Apple went further, it went beyond its dealership and announced AppleLink Personal Edition for users in 1988.

Bright and colorful, if possibly a bit patronizing, Apple's eWorld including support discussions - image credit: Apple

You do not want to go down the rabbit hole that Apple did with this, although if you remember AOL and ever wondered how it started, this was a key element. What's important now is that eventually Apple's forum offering was part of eWorld.

Today the most notable part of eWorld is how the limited internet support it eventually added was codenamed Golden Gate. That would be 31 years before it reused that code name for macOS 27.

This eWorld was a flop and in 1996, then-CEO Gil Amelio killed it. In an explanatory message to eWorld users, Diana Keith, then Apple's Director of Internet Productions said:

The way we see it, the smartest move for Apple to make is to greatly expand our presence on the Internet. And the best way to structure that presence is with a portfolio of web sites and services for particular customer groups-not a general online service like eWorld.

Effective March 31, 1996, eWorld was gone. And then in 1998, there came Apple Tech Exchange.

From tech to consumers

"Apple Tech Exchange" was definitely a name for its time, as back then the firm was solely a computer company. Even its name then was Apple Computer, Inc. But just as the company moved on, just as it became a consumer technology firm, so its online support developed to match.

That company move would become obvious in 2007 with the iPhone and with the name change to just "Apple" in 2007. But it started with the iMac and the iPod, and in between both, Apple repositioned its forums.

During 2000, Apple Tech Exchange was out, and Apple Discussions was in. It's not clear now whether this was solely a rebranding or whether Apple actually started over again with its forums.

But whatever it did, Apple did it for about a decade. It wasn't until early August 2010 that users started to notice something was wrong.

Apple Support Communities

This time Apple did definitely retain all of the postings that had been done in Apple Discussions. In 2010, the new Apple Support Communities forums were the old Apple Discussions with a new coat of paint.

Whatever problem you had with Apple devices, someone else had gone through it too, and would answer your question - image credit: Apple.

That's not really fair, since it was this August 2010 rebrand that also gave users new abilities. From this point on, they could have a personalized profile, plus a custom picture and avatar.

There may also have been more to it behind the scenes, though, as in the weeks leading up to this change, some users were having difficulties with Apple Discussions. Then Apple had begun teasing the changeover as a "major upgrade."

"Apple Discussions" was definitely less technical-sounding than "Apple Tech Exchange," and surely Apple was trying to attract more general users. But then "Apple Discussions" sounds like it's for chatting about the company, not for getting actual help and advice.

So the name "Apple Support Communities" tried to do both jobs. You'd know what you were getting, in the sense that there would be support.

Plus you'd know that this was a hopefully welcoming space for, well, Apple discussions.

You can argue over whether Apple thought this deeply about the name. And of course you can debate how useful the service was. In 2026, it was a pretty good historical reference.

That historical record will be gone soon enough. Apple has confirmed to us that not only are the forums getting shut down, they're being taken completely offline.

Apple Support Communities was not the busiest online forum for Apple discussions. It was arguably not the best for finding answers through a sea of snarky comments.

And, it was full of folks that pointed to all of the people complaining about an issue that they have, citing the hundreds of posts. In reality, those hundreds were usually the same person complaining in 2/3 of the posts.

Yet still, if we won't miss the comments, it's also true that Apple Support Communities has helped us out of a jam more than once.

And that's why this will be missed.

items.title: Apple supplier confirms involvement in Apple AI glasses, AirPods with cameras
items.content_html:
Apple's long-rumored smart glasses and AirPods with cameras are still on the way, according to one Chinese supplier's earnings report.

While companies tend to avoid spoiling future product plans when discussing their quarterly results, not everyone goes to the lengths Apple does for corporate secrecy. For one firm in China, the opposite seems to be the case.

The filing by TCB Devices for its Q3 2026 financial results, as covered by iFeng, is fairly straightforward. It starts off advising of increased demand in the semiconductor, optical communication, and data center industries.

However, the report later says that TCB Devices had participated with Apple's "AI glasses and new smart earphone projects." To TCB, that will help improve related business sectors, such as precision welding assembly and machine vision inspection.

This is a direct reference to Apple Glass, as well as AirPods with cameras.

TCB's admission of being involved in unannounced Apple projects is an unusual move, and could well result in a reprimand in the near future.

In 2021, Hyundai confirmed that it was in talks with Apple about potentially building an Apple Car. Apple promptly backed away from the discussions over the lack of secrecy, potentially costing Hyundai billions in lost sales.

Intelligent headwear

Apple's smart glasses ambitions have an end goal of bringing a full augmented reality smart glasses experience to consumers. However, that will be a project that won't emerge for quite a few years.

Instead, the first release of Apple Glass will be as AI smart glasses without AR, or seemingly any display elements at all. That product is currently anticipated for release sometime in late 2027.

While it won't have AR, the initial Apple Glass release will still work with Siri AI and Apple Intelligence, using a microphone and speaker as well as a set of low-resolution cameras. The intention is to capture the environment, feeding that into Visual Intelligence, and using that to help answer the user's queries and prompts.

Though they sound like a different product, AirPods with cameras are really the same sort of concept, without the spectacles. Low-resolution cameras in each AirPods earpiece capture the world, and again, feed that into Apple Intelligence on a nearby iPhone.

Unusually, Apple itself has leaked the existence of the special AirPods, including code references and a video clip in a developer beta.

items.title: Unpatched exploit allows malicious iOS apps to steal data
items.content_html:
Crypto exchange Binance is warning iPhone users of a security vulnerability in iOS that could allow a malicious app to steal data from other apps on the device.

Finance apps have a big interest in maintaining security, especially when it comes to their own apps. Sometimes that protectiveness results in a warning that affects the operating system itself.

In a post to X on November 10, crypto app Binance warns of a vulnerability that affects multiple versions of iOS, including iOS 26.7.1, 27.0.1, and iOS 27.2 This time, it's not a problem specific to Binance's app, but instead it is referred to as an "iOS-level issue," affecting practically all apps, reports Yahoo Finance.

Given the name "worse_query," the vulnerability can allow a malicious app to read local files from other apps, otherwise known as a sandbox escape. To Binance, the vulnerability means that the seed phrases, private keys, and login credentials are at risk for all apps in the Apple ecosystem.

Binance advises that users should delete apps installed from untrusted sources, such as those that are sideloaded or have manually-signed IPAs. All updates to iOS and apps should be performed, bringing them to the latest official versions.

If users suspect they have had a breach of their Binance account, the exchange says that they should transfer their funds to a new wallet created on a clean device, and to reset all active login sessions.

The timing of the warning comes after Binance suffered a major breach, leading to the draining of $6.3 billion worth of crypto. However, the warning appears to be completely unrelated to that breach.

An irresponsible disclosure?

Researchers forcequit and 0xjohnny released the escape on Sunday, according to Hacker News. At this time, it seems that the issue hasn't yet been fixed by Apple.

On November 9, Apple released updates for iOS 27.2.1 and iOS 26.7.3. However, the security content report for version 27.2.1 doesn't include any descriptions that match that of the flaw.

Apple is also currently on its first developer beta of iOS 27.3. That was issued on November 3, long before the researchers published the exploit.

In follow-up posts, forcequit claims that worse_query was not patched in iOS 27.2.1 nor 27.3 beta 1.

This seems to be an unusual situation, as typically researchers provide Apple and other software providers with a grace period to fix issues. Under a normal responsible disclosure, this would give Apple time to create and release a security update as part of a patch.

As part of their November 8 conversations on X, forcequit posts a screenshot from October 10, saying Apple will review their report soon. However, the note adds that, despite it usually taking seven days to review reports, Apple said it's taking "a bit longer."

Responding to a comment that releasing early may not have been a good idea, due to the potential of receiving a bug bounty, forcequit said they didn't mind missing any potential bounty payments. Especially when they considered Apple was "stalling" on its response.

Even if Apple didn't respond to that report, the spreading of the exploit's existence by Binance means Apple has to move fast to plug that security hole anyway.

items.title: iPhone Duo photography overview: Great cameras that suffer in extreme low light
items.content_html:
If you're holding off on an iPhone Duo solely because of camera concerns, you probably don't need to, but you will miss the advantages offered by pro iPhones.

I've spent the past few weeks thinking hard about my place as a photographer and my iPhone's position in it. There is no doubt that Apple's iPhone has been a camera powerhouse for over a decade, but I'm increasingly aware of how few "pro" features I actually need.

I never needed to confront this reality directly since Apple's most desirable iPhone was also the most "pro." I could grab whatever iPhone Pro Max and be happy knowing I'd have every photography feature available without compromise.

Then Apple revealed iPhone Duo.

I wanted to write this for anyone wondering exactly where iPhone Duo fits in as an iPhone camera. This story is not meant to convince you whether or not to purchase Apple's foldable, as I've already made those calls in the main review.

Long story short, there are a lot of reasons to consider or reject iPhone Duo, but the camera system isn't one of them. There will be features you'll miss if you're coming from any recent pro iPhone, but they won't make or break your experience.

Let's get into the iPhone Duo as a camera.

Where the iPhone Duo camera is actually worse

The iPhone Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system with a Main and Ultra Wide camera. Users will take 95% of their pictures with the Main camera and the rest with the Ultra Wide.

I'm glad the Ultra Wide is there for macro shots and some interesting artistic angles, but it will once again not be the focus of this discussion. It's the same Ultra Wide camera that is used in the iPhone 18 Pro, so there really isn't much to say.

The Fusion Main camera on iPhone Duo has a smaller sensor at 1/1.56 inch versus 1/1.3 inch on the iPhone 18 Pro Max. It also lacks 100% Focus Pixels and uses what Apple calls Hybrid Focus Pixels.

The iPhone Duo Main Camera also has a slower aperture at f/1.6 versus the iPhone 18 Pro's variable aperture starting at f/1.48. That said, the default f/1.8 is slower and has a longer focus distance versus the iPhone Duo.

These specs primarily affect the iPhone Duo's performance in low light. The spec sheet showed this early on in my early analysis, and actual use proved it out.

Unless you can literally take a photo side-by-side at the exact moment with an iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone Duo, you'll never notice the difference in good lighting. Even then, you'll have to open the photos up in image editors to pixel-peep and find where the sharpness falls off on iPhone Duo.

Now I realize a lot of photography writers talk about lighting in a passing fashion, so I want to be a little more specific. What constitutes "good" to "average" light is what you will encounter in the daytime or in a well-lit room.

Well-lit is relative, and I'm not going to throw lumens at you, but instead consider well-lit to be a room with the lights on where fine details are visible to the naked eye. You could easily read a book, spot a detail in a photo hanging on the wall, or see the texture of a person's skin in this light.

Medium to low light is similar to what you might experience outside before a severe thunderstorm or inside with the overhead light turned off, but accent lighting is still on. People's faces will be partially or totally cast in shadow, fine details are lost without getting closer, and colors appear more muted.

From dim to pure darkness, like low to no light sources, iPhone Duo will perform worse versus pro models. For example, the first time I noticed poor low-light performance with iPhone Duo was at a Halloween party a week after receiving my device.

I took dozens of photos prior to then in plenty of lighting conditions and noticed zero problems with the camera's performance. It wasn't until ISO cranked itself up to 1,000 and started setting shutter speeds over half a second that things became less ideal.

To be clear, you can still take photos in low to no light with an iPhone Duo, but moving targets are a no-go unless you want motion blur. Still images captured with long exposure in Night Mode are still usable.

The iPhone 18 Pro isn't immune from these low-to-no-light conditions, however, it has superior light gathering capabilities. The need to fall back onto longer exposures occurs later, though not much later.

After using an iPhone Pro for years, I've been spoiled by the low-light performance and took it for granted. I was caught somewhat by surprise at that Halloween party and had to adjust the types of photos I pursued.

In the end, I still took plenty of usable photos at that party, but I had to plan things out more than usual. It's not a significant compromise, and I fully expect it'll be rectified in version 2.

I want to emphasize how dim it has to be for things to start becoming messy. If there is a light source nearby, like a lamp, in an otherwise dark space, you'll still take mostly sharp photos if your subject is in the light.

Imagine trying to take a photo of the person next to you at a movie theater — that's the conditions I'm talking about when I say low-to-no light.

Night Mode is aggressive and can often be toggled off when on the edge of kicking in. An ISO of 1,000 or 2,000 isn't ideal, but the noise produced at these levels is often smoothed or produces an interesting result.

Anyway, three weeks later, I can honestly say the worse performance in low light and the lack of an optical telephoto are all I miss on iPhone Duo. Neither make the device less desirable, though I am fully aware of what I'm missing out on when those shots present themselves and I can't take them the way that I want.

I haven't mentioned the lack of Pro Tools, ProRAW, ProRes, LiDAR, and spatial capture because they feel quite minor to this discussion. If you require those features above all else, the iPhone Duo isn't even a part of the conversation.

Even though I enjoy taking professional photos with absolute control, I tend to save that kind of photography for my full-sized camera. I've increasingly leaned on Photographic Styles on iPhone, so the lack of these pro features aren't something I miss.

Your miles may vary.

Where the iPhone Duo camera excels

If you're coming from any iPhone that isn't the iPhone 18 Pro Max, there are elements of the iPhone Duo camera that are better. As I covered in the iPhone Duo review, there are improved aspects related to the better photographic pipeline.

The A20 Pro has an improved image signal processor that Apple tweaks with every iteration. The latest generation appears to have changes to how it calculates noise removal in shadows, plus there's new white balance controls.

There's also Photographic Styles 3 which include texture control options. iPhone Duo also has the new manual white balance control option, though that's available on iPhone 18 Pro as well.

I've found that the combination of Photographic Styles 3 and white balance controls provide enough differentiation versus older iPhones. In some circumstances I'm able to take better photos than what I could on my iPhone 17 Pro Max.

The closer minimum focus distance is also a boon, though one I'm aware will go away in future models. I'm able to get closer to a subject before switching to macro mode, which is more desirable in several situations.

Having the ability to control white balance in the default camera app has been very useful. I can capture photos that look closer to what the naked eye perceives thanks to being able to say what my lighting conditions are.

The iPhone has always been able to do a good job at managing white balance on its own, but it doesn't do a perfect job. Sometimes it compensates for the wrong elements and can wash out an image or render the colors incorrectly.

Overall, the iPhone Duo camera experience is good enough that no one will notice a problem. Sure, low light isn't perfect, but depending on which iPhone you're upgrading from, you probably won't notice much difference there either.

About that Fusion Ultra Wide camera

I don't want to keep ignoring the Fusion Ultra Wide simply because it's identical to the iPhone 18 Pro. Funny enough, you won't be using it as often unless you deliberately want a macro photo.

Sometimes, you'll get better results when sticking with the Fusion Main camera versus switching to macro mode. The improved depth of field and light gathering abilities will always result in more dynamic photos.

That said, macro mode is such a specific style that it is best used when getting very close to a small subject. It can bring out details even the naked eye doesn't see, like textures in a material.

The Fusion Ultra Wide camera benefits from the same systems as the Fusion Main camera. The A20 processor, Photographic Styles 3, and white balance control are all available here.

Unique photographic aspects of iPhone Duo

There are four cameras on the iPhone Duo: Fusion Main, Fusion Ultra Wide, outer selfie, and inner selfie.

I already detailed the other cameras available in the main iPhone Duo review. You'll be taking standard selfies with the outer camera and using the inner camera for FaceTime calls.

The iPhone Duo also has the ability to show your subject a preview of the photo on the outer display or show Snoopy to catch children's attention. The Kid Cue feature has become an instant favorite for taking photos of the families of all ages in my life.

Smart Take has also been an incredible boon since I'm not the type to carry a tripod, selfie stick, or any kind of stand. It's nice being able to just set up the iPhone to take pics whether you're home alone, on a hike, or away from other people in general.

Not to mention other people are just bad at taking photos. No really, go learn the basics of framing a shot and stop including people's legs in every photo.

Anyway, the iPhone Duo may not have the "best" camera system in an iPhone, but it has a really good one with unique abilities. Most people will never even realize the camera system was compromised to achieve the needed device thinness.

I've noticed that I tend to take photos with the device closed. The tiny form factor and full-screen outer display viewfinder with Camera Control really make it feel more immersive.

When framing is of utmost importance, you'll need to open the iPhone to see the entire photo. The view on the outer display is punched in slightly.

Using the inner display for taking pictures can feel a little awkward, but you get over that feeling after a few uses. It does feel a little counterintuitive to hold the device in a vertical orientation to take horizontally-framed photos though.

I really like having the ability to take selfies using the outer display as a viewfinder for the rear cameras. That feature has come in handy, though it does take some practice to learn how to properly frame yourself.

I've written 2,000 more words to say what I already said in the review — if you're considering the iPhone Duo and are concerned about the camera at all, don't be. As always with Apple, specs don't tell the whole story and the iPhone Duo is a capable and very interesting camera system.

Now let's see what Apple does with version 2.

items.title: Thai politicians question Apple over iPhone spyware alerts
items.content_html:
Following Apple's issuing of spyware alerts to politicians' iPhones in the country, officials in Thailand have met with the company as they aim to strengthen security.

These spyware alerts were sent on October 29, 2026, at around the same time the same warnings were sent to officials in Germany. Those warnings also followed a wave of spyware activity in August 2026, that saw Apple alerting people in 110 countries.

Now according to Bloomberg, Apple representatives have met with Thailand's Ministry of Digital Economy and Society. Ahead of the talks, Minister Chaichanok Chidchob described the cyber threat as being unprecedented in scale.

While no details are expected to be released from the meeting with Apple, the minister said that it was part of a series of discussions. Following the Apple talks, the ministry is to work with the country's National Security Council, the National Cyber Security Agency, plus hardware and software firms across Thailand.

Chaichanok said that the intention was to gather a comprehensive picture of the attacks before implementing a security plan. It's not known whether that plan will be revealed, but the minister said he expects it to be ready the week of November 16, 2026.

Who Apple warns

Apple will of course not detail how it determines whether there is a spyware attack. It has said that its processes concern "mercenary spyware attacks [that are] vastly more sophisticated than regular cybercriminal activity."

Once Apple has reason to believe that there may have been a cyber attack on iPhones, it issues what the company calls "high-confidence alerts." It does not and cannot "achieve absolute certainty," but will issue threat notifications to the iPhones believed to be affected.

Since it began doing this back in 2021, Apple says that it has alerted users in over 150 countries.

items.title: Apple Support Community Forums are shutting down
items.content_html:
As of Tuesday, new forum posts cannot be made to Apple's Support Community Forums and the entire website will be closed on November 20. Apple did not provide a reason for the closure.

The likely reason for closing the forums is due to the emergence of communities like Reddit and Discord on top of LLM use. Apple Support also uses artificial intelligence to parse queries.

The good news is, AppleInsider will continue to offer detailed articles on how to solve any problem, plus you can use our forums to ask for help from our staff and many knowledgeable forum members.

items.title: PROLED MacBook Pro teardown shows how the glowing Apple logo works
items.content_html:
While the PROLED MacBook Pro is more repairable, the returning glowing Apple logo isn't something you'll want to mess with.

In October 2026, Apple finally brought a touchscreen to the Mac in the form of the PROLED MacBook Pro. The revamped models also come with reinforced hinges, Dynamic Island, and an even thinner chassis.

However, the glowing Apple logo on the back is the most easily noticeable change. It's a callback that makes the PROLED MacBook Pro feel instantly familiar to anyone who's owned an Apple laptop made between 1999 and 2015.

However, the underlying technology has changed considerably with the PROLED MacBook Pro. Since the tandem OLED panel removed the need for an LED backlight, Apple had to get creative to make its logo shine again.

As iFixit reveals in its teardown of the 14-inch PROLED MacBook Pro, Apple used four LEDs and a diffuser to create the glowing effect. Thanks to a reflective coating, meanwhile, the logo acts as a two-way mirror, glowing whenever the display is on.

However, if the Apple logo stops lighting up, you might have to replace the whole screen assembly. When the publication attempted to open the PROLED XDR display, the glass layer shattered and delaminated, effectively breaking the OLED panel.

Because the glowing Apple logo sits right behind the tandem OLED display, it will be difficult for anyone to replace it without damaging the screen. Many other components are not user-replaceable, either.

As with all Apple Silicon laptops, the NAND chips are soldered to the main logic board. The same goes for the M5 Pro or M5 Max system-on-chip, the SD-card reader, and even the HDMI port. The battery is also held in place with removable pull tabs rather than screws.

Some parts, meanwhile, are easier to replace, like the USB-C ports and the MagSafe 3 connector, all of which are screwed in rather than soldered to the logic board. However, you will need to remove the logic board itself to replace any of the ports that are screwed in.

The PROLED MacBook Pro is also easier to open, with the bottom case held in place by four screws, down from eight on the base M6 MacBook Pro. Apple also made the bottom case 44 grams lighter, as it now weighs 364 grams, compared to 456 with the preceding MacBook Pro design.

Beyond the weight and display upgrades, the PROLED MacBook Pro is not all that different from the standard M6 MacBook Pro. Even the display hinge, which Apple says was redesigned for touch-based input, looks almost identical to the one on older MacBook Pros.

The logic board itself doesn't look all that different, either, and the trackpad is only slightly smaller on the PROLED MacBook Pro. You'll get the same macOS experience, just with a touchscreen.

Though Apple did still prioritize form over function in terms of design, swapping parts on the PROLED MacBook Pro won't cause any pairing issues. The touchscreen, display, and Touch ID sensor remain functional even after the logic board is replaced with a different one.

In terms of overall repairability, iFixit gave the PROLED MacBook Pro a five out of ten rating. This is up one point from the earlier MacBook Pro design. However, it's also one point lower than the MacBook Neo.

items.title: New AirPods firmware has been released by Apple
items.content_html:
If you've got a set of AirPods with the H2 chip, it has an update to firmware version 9B47. That means the AirPods 4, AirPods 5, AirPods Pro 2, AirPods Pro 3, and AirPods Max 2 are able to be updated.

There is no manual process for updating AirPods. Connecting them to power and leaving them near your iPhone can sometimes trigger an update.

items.title: Apple's 'Harbor' app will make running local AI across multiple Macs trivial
items.content_html:
An app presently called "Harbor" will help turn multiple Macs into a private AI inference server, keeping data local while also making the process of creating an AI server much easier.

The Mac has become a very useful tool for AI research, but it could be even more useful. Apple is working on an app that can make it easier to run large language models (LLMs) locally, so long as you have enough processing power and memory available.

Formerly known as Fabric, Harbor is the app that creates a private AI inference server on a Mac, according to Aaronp613 on X. It is capable of running open-weight models on the Mac itself, and apparently is extremely user-friendly.

Apple is working on a new app called Harbor

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon— your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.

Set up in minutes, not hours Harbor automatically detects your devices over Thunderbolt 5 to form a cluster. Plug in, start, and you're running— no manual configuration, no command line, no infrastructure expertise required.

Download and run models directly Browse, download, and load open-weight models from within the app. Harbor handles model management so you can focus on the work, not the setup.

Cluster for scale Connect two or more Thunderbolt 5-capable Mac computers and Harbor pools their unified memory into a single inference resource. Run models that exceed any single computer's capacity, or serve more concurrent requests across your cluster.

Harbor is currently in a private preview under the Claris brand.

— Aaron (@aaronp613) November 10, 2026

The installation requires just a few minutes to complete, with seemingly no need to manually configure anything or use a command line. Harbor manages the model on behalf of the user, including handling the downloads directly.

If there is more than one Mac available, they can be connected as a cluster over Thunderbolt 5. These are automatically detected by Harbor, which deals with the inter-device connection and the now larger pool of unified memory.

End users shouldn't expect to see the app anytime soon. Harbor is currently in "private preview" under Apple's Claris brand.

A massive help for AI development

Like pretty much any new technology trend, it can be difficult to get into working with AI. Especially if you don't want to deal with cloud-based services.

Not everyone wants to simply hand their data over to OpenAI or Anthropic in exchange for their services. Making a local LLM server eliminates that, but at a fairly high financial cost of new hardware.

But at the same time, there's also the work that needs to be put in to get the server up and running. If you have multiple Macs available, clustering them together to handle tougher workloads is a possibility.

Apple has already provided some software assistance, with MLX using Thunderbolt networking to cluster devices together for this purpose. Later, Apple made changes to macOS and MLX to include Thunderbolt 5 support as well as the introduction of GPU-based neural accelerator support.

In October 2026, it also detailed a new Minions system that uses idle GPUs in Apple Silicon Macs and turning them into a dynamic virtual GPU cloud.

Harbor appears to be an attempt focused on making the process of getting things going, rather than improving the performance of AI. While it may not make queries run faster, it's a change that should make the entire system much easier to get going in the first place.

items.title: If you're getting dizzy using PROLED MacBook Pro, you are not alone
items.content_html:
The new MacBook Pro uses pulse width modulation that is inducing eye strain, and headaches for some new buyers. Here's what pulse width modulation is, why it may cause problems for some users, and what you can do about it.

In short, the PROLED MacBook Pro is constantly strobing the user at a bad combination of frequency and amplitude. It's not as obvious as a flashing light at a rave or party, or light filtered through helicopter blades, but it is happening constantly, at close range.

Some people are susceptible to potentially serious health issues from those strobing lights. Others may have existing health conditions that are aggravated by the flashing lights.

Video game publishers have warned about this kind of thing for some time, and the concept has been used by trolls to attack people with epilepsy. The health issues aren't as bad as what the Apple Vision Pro can induce given the wide field of vision that headset fills, but given that this is the first time that the technology has come to the MacBook Pro, it's worth talking about again.

Here's why that all matters, and who it matters to.

Health issues from strobing lights, and who is affected

We are not medical doctors here at AppleInsider, but this author had a child that was profoundly epileptic, and we did talk to neurologists before writing this article for Apple Vision Pro first, and now again for this version of the article for MacBook Pro.

We're comfortable writing this article given this mix of practical experience and professional consultation.

There are three main types of health impacts from strobing lights — flicker vertigo, photosensitive epilepsy, and general photosensitivity.

Flicker Vertigo happens at refresh rates between 1Hz and 20Hz, and can cause disorientation, nausea, and rapid eye movement.

It was first spotted in early helicopters, watching the sun strobe through a rotating helicopter blade. It is less common on the road, but still can be seen by the driver and passengers as the sun filters through trees as a car drives through a lightly wooded area.

Flicker Vertigo is common, but fortunately the symptoms vanish when the strobing stops. It is not incredibly relevant to MacBook Pro owners, unless they are hit with maliciously crafted content — which as we've mentioned happens from time to time.

Photosensitive epilepsy is far less common, but far more dangerous. While sensitivities vary, any strobing can induce a seizure in folks with photosensitive epilepsy. The individual circumstances and severity of the seizure can vary, person to person.

And, it is possible for somebody to not have any other outward signs of epilepsy, and still be susceptible to specific photosensitive triggers that they previously weren't aware of.

Other health conditions can be aggravated by strobing light. A very high percentage of traumatic brain injury sufferers report photosensitivity, as do people with migraines, frequent tension headaches, or cluster headaches.

If you've ever been told you have photophobia, the Apple Vision Pro and the new PROLED MacBook Pro are probably not for you.

Sensitivity to strobing lights is also aggravated by fatigue of any sort, diet, time of exposure to the strobing and a host of other situations. If you're well-rested, you may not be sensitive to strobing lights.

If you've skipped a meal, are pulling an all-nighter in front of your MacBook Pro, and didn't get any sleep the previous night, that's about the worst-case scenario.

In all of these cases, the situation is aggravated as more of the user's field of vision is impacted by the strobing. In the case of the Apple Vision Pro, the user's entire field of vision is covered by the strobing from the Pulse Width Modulation used to control the screens' brightness and color mix.

For the new MacBook Pro, it's not the entire field of vision, but it is a wide one. The pulse width modulation, which is not the same as the screen refresh rate, is running at 240Hz on the new MacBook Pro, with a 56% flicker amplitude. This is the same as it is on modern iPhones, but it is also on a much larger screen.

For instance, Pulse width modulation exists in non-OLED screens too. The M4 Pro Mini-LED MacBook has a 14,880 Hz pulse width modulation, which is better for nearly everybody.

Clearly, not everybody is impacted by strobing lights, and even so, frequency sensitivity can vary. This is good, considering the LED light bulbs that have replaced incandescent lights flicker, although less than the fluorescent bulbs that were a stop-gap between the Edison incandescent bulb and the newer LED.

That's cold comfort to the people who are hit, though. And, it's why Genius Bars we've spoken to are getting complaints, and retailers are seeing returns of the hardware at a bit higher rate than normal.

Just because you're not having an issue, doesn't mean that it's not a problem.

What is Pulse Width Modulation?

There is a lot to Pulse Width Modulation in electronics as a whole, but as it pertains to Apple hardware, Pulse Width Modulation is what Apple uses by default to regulate the brightness of individual color cells in the eye displays.

An incandescent bulb that can dim throws off fewer photons when at a lower wattage, roughly proportional to the magnitude of the cut in power. Provide half the power to an incandescent bulb, and it will be about half as bright.

It does not turn off quickly and strobe. Incandescents just emits fewer photons because of the lower power.

In an OLED display such as that used in the MacBook Pro, brightness control and color mixing is accomplished by turning individual color cells on and off very quickly. If full power, constantly, is being applied to a color cell, then that cell is "on time" or at a 100% duty cycle, and is fully bright.

Pulse width modulation and duty cycle example - credit circuitdigest.com

While there is an overall screen refresh frequency factor to consider as it pertains to health, in short, given a fixed frequency, to reduce the brightness, at default settings, the color cell is extremely rapidly turned on and off. A 50% duty cycle has the cell on or off half of the time, and is about half the brightness. It also effectively strobes the user at a different frequency than the display as a whole is doing.

Pulse Width Modulation has been used in OLED iPhones since the iPhone X, and it is vital to the operation of the screen. It has always been a concern at some level, to some people. However, the iPhone is a hand-held device, not occupying the a large percentage of field of vision that the Apple Vision Pro and PROLED MacBook Pro maintain.

How bad is this?

We've been watching for reports of photosensitivity since the new iPad mini and PROLED MacBook Pro launched, like we did for Apple Vision Pro. There are periodic social media reports of headaches and fatigue.

The advice is clear from the doctors we've spoken to, and from Apple itself. If you start feeling strange in any way while using Apple Vision Pro, and now MacBook Pro, stop using it, and schedule an appoint with your doctor.

And, watch for symptoms in folks that you care about that are new owners. It's easy to get over-excited about new technology, and use it for far more than you should in the early days.

Apple has help for this on the iPhone, but not yet the MacBook Pro.

No good way to reduce strobing from the MacBook Pro

There's a setting on iPad mini, and iPhones after the iPhone 17, called Display Pulse Smoothing. It lives in Accessibility, and when the feature is on, it turns off pulse width modulation at lower brightness, and uses voltage dimming to provide a different way to dim the OLED display.

This setting is not in macOS. At least, not yet.

As of November 10, 2026, if you know you're sensitive to Pulse Width Modulation or strobing, do not buy the new MacBook Pro with PROLED display. Stick with the previous models.

items.title: Nintendo won't let you log in with a linked Apple account soon
items.content_html:
Effective January 26, 2027, you will be unable to use a linked Google or Apple account to sign in to a Nintendo Account, and it won't be possible to create a new Nintendo Account using either. Instead, use a Passkey, or change your account information.
